sections.title: Design inference and evidential reach
sections.rationale: This section tests the form of the design inference, its fossil evidence, and the acknowledged gap between an inferred architect and a specifically good Christian God.

sections.title: Cosmos, providence, and human significance
sections.rationale: This section weighs cosmic beginnings and human significance against destructive scale, evolutionary contingency, providential flexibility, and the universe’s apparent waste.

sections.title: Evolution and scientific method
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute what evolutionary evidence establishes, how adaptation and loss bear on origins, and whether revision and disagreement strengthen or weaken scientific explanation.

sections.title: Morality, altruism, and human value
sections.rationale: This section compares divine grounding of objective value with social, evolutionary, and pluralist accounts of moral judgment and human worth.

sections.title: Evil, scripture, and fallen-world theodicy
sections.rationale: The goodness burden is tested through biblical violence, natural suffering, fallenness, divine judgment, and the charge that rebellion theology worsens rather than answers evil.

sections.title: Incarnation, atonement, and freedom
sections.rationale: The exchange directly tests whether incarnation supplies divine solidarity, whether substitution can address guilt, and whether salvation preserves responsibility and intellectual freedom.

sections.title: Ideology, charity, and public consequences
sections.rationale: The closing exchange compares religious and secular coercion, charitable motives and effects, and the political consequences attributed to belief and disbelief.

balanceRationale: The source contains two more con than pro moves overall. The four con moves in the cosmos section independently address cosmic destruction, providential unfalsifiability, species extinction, and cosmic waste, while the four con ideology moves separately address authoritarian theology, Mother Teresa’s institutional effects, ethical plurality, and the classification of Nazism; none duplicates another selected inference.

sectionRationales.rationale: A fourth pro row is required because specified complexity states the inference rule, architect-only limits its conclusion, design-and-faith explains why that limit leaves faith intact, and fossil-record limits supplies a distinct empirical application.

A fourth con row is required because cosmic destruction challenges benevolence, providential flexibility challenges falsifiability, extinction challenges special design through natural history, and cosmic waste combines origin alternatives with the universe’s projected fate.

The fourth pro row is required because the multi-example evidence challenge, atheism’s claimed dependence on unguided origins, eye-loss versus eye-origin, and the microevolution scope limit are four independent inferences.

The fourth pro row is required because divine goodness as a standard, the challenge to objective atheist morality, claimed worldview consequences, and evolution’s morally mixed outcomes make independent normative and explanatory arguments.

The four selected con moves independently challenge biblical history, explicit genocidal commands, inherited rebellion and punishment, and the naturalistic explanation of suffering; each tests a different premise of divine goodness.
The two moves per side form distinct but linked exchanges over incarnation, substitution, forgiveness, responsibility, and the intellectual cost of promised certainty.

A fourth con row is required because authoritarian divine rule, Mother Teresa’s policy effects, atheism’s ethical plurality, and Nazism’s religious entanglements are separate replies to distinct parts of the parity claim.
